data.name: Electronics Circuits Simulator
data.detailed_description:
Learn electronic circuits in a new and exciting way and increase your understanding of basic electronic circuits.

Seven complete levels to assess your knowledge of basic electronic circuits including Series Parallel Resistor circuits, Resistor Capacitor (RC) filters, Graetz Bridges, Wheatstone bridges, Weighted summing amplifiers, Transistor switches and Oscillator circuits.

This game complements the Circuit Warz game which is also on STEAM. It allows you to practice each of the 7 levels before you play the main game.

Topics covered include

Current and Voltage
Resistance and Resistors
Capacitance and Capacitors
Alternating Current
Semiconductors
Transistors
Diodes
Ohms Law
Equivalent resistance

reviews.review:
Electronics Circuits Simulator takes a noticeably different approach from most games carrying the simulation label. Rather than building its experience around management, storytelling, or open-ended experimentation, it focuses on teaching fundamental electronics through interactive circuit exercises. Developed by Arttu Tuovinen, Alan Bourhis, and Michael Callaghan and published by Michael Callaghan, it is best understood as a compact educational application that uses game-like interaction to make basic electrical principles more approachable. Its appeal is therefore strongest for students, electronics hobbyists, and curious players who want practical exposure to circuit concepts.

The experience is organized around seven levels covering different circuit configurations. These include series-parallel resistor circuits, resistor-capacitor filters, Graetz bridges, Wheatstone bridges, weighted summing amplifiers, transistor switches, and oscillator circuits. Although seven levels make the overall package fairly small, there is reasonable variety in the subjects being introduced. The progression exposes players to both passive components and semiconductor-based systems, gradually moving from relatively straightforward resistor relationships toward circuits involving transistors and oscillation.

The educational material reaches beyond simply recognizing individual circuit layouts. Players encounter concepts involving voltage, current, resistance, capacitance, alternating current, resistors, capacitors, diodes, semiconductors, and transistors. Ohm's Law and equivalent resistance also form important parts of the underlying knowledge. For beginners, this interactive approach can make abstract principles easier to visualize. Seeing how components relate within a circuit can provide a more intuitive understanding than memorizing formulas without practical context.

Its greatest strength is the direct connection between theory and application. Electronics is a subject where mathematical relationships can initially seem disconnected from physical components, and an interactive simulator provides an opportunity to connect those ideas. Understanding why changing resistance influences electrical behavior or seeing the role of a diode within a bridge circuit can reinforce lessons that might otherwise remain purely theoretical. Players who already have some introductory electronics knowledge are likely to gain the most from the exercises because they can immediately relate the challenges to concepts they have encountered elsewhere.

The game also functions as a practice companion to Circuit Warz, with its seven circuit topics intended to help users prepare for related challenges. This relationship helps explain why the simulator is so focused instead of trying to become a comprehensive virtual electronics laboratory. Anyone expecting the freedom and sophistication of professional circuit-design software will find the feature set restrictive. There is no enormous component catalog or expansive engineering workspace here. The emphasis remains firmly on learning and practicing a predetermined collection of fundamental circuit concepts.

As entertainment, the experience is considerably more specialized. There is satisfaction in successfully understanding and completing an electronics problem, but that reward comes primarily from learning rather than traditional gameplay excitement. There is little reason for someone uninterested in electronics to spend much time with it. The relatively limited number of exercises also means that longevity is modest once the available material has been understood. More circuits, expanded tutorials, additional difficulty levels, and a larger experimental sandbox could have transformed the concept into a much more substantial educational package.

Presentation is functional and serves the instructional purpose without becoming a major attraction itself. This straightforward design keeps the player's attention on circuit behavior and the problem being studied, although the overall experience feels comparatively basic when measured against newer educational software. Better visual explanations and more detailed guidance would particularly benefit complete beginners. Electronics can become complicated quickly, and topics such as transistor operation, alternating current, and oscillators are difficult to fully understand through brief interactive exercises alone.

For that reason, Electronics Circuits Simulator works better as supplementary learning material than as a substitute for structured electronics education. A student could use it alongside classroom instruction, textbooks, tutorials, or practical laboratory work, while a hobbyist might use it as a lightweight introduction before moving into more sophisticated simulation tools. It can demonstrate important relationships, but it cannot provide the depth necessary to fully explain every electrical principle represented by its circuits. Players willing to research unfamiliar concepts independently will obtain considerably more value from it.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially categorized with a Steam Deck Verified or Playable rating. Because the software was designed primarily around a conventional PC interface and has no official Deck verification, it should be regarded as unsupported or unverified for Steam Deck rather than assumed to provide a seamless handheld experience. It may potentially run through SteamOS compatibility technology, but users should expect possible control, interface, or usability limitations and should not treat native handheld optimization as one of its features.

Overall, Electronics Circuits Simulator is a niche but purposeful educational experience. Its limited content and basic presentation prevent it from becoming a definitive electronics simulator, yet its coverage of resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, AC concepts, Ohm's Law, bridges, filters, switches, and oscillators gives beginners several worthwhile areas to explore. The game is most valuable when approached with the intention of learning rather than seeking conventional entertainment. For the right audience, interacting with circuits provides a useful bridge between theoretical explanations and practical understanding, even though a larger collection of exercises and stronger teaching tools would greatly improve its long-term usefulness.

Rating: 6/10
